core: Working definition of secondary prevention, attributed to the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021): early detection of existing disease with a view to arresting or delaying the progression of the disease and its effects
The idea: find it sooner, treat it sooner, argued with an original example
The three tools named: screening tests, early diagnosis, and early treatment, each with one line and an original example
Screening named factually: testing people who have no symptoms, plus the honest note on screening trade-offs (false positives, false negatives, overdiagnosis)
Secondary versus the other levels: early stage vs before onset vs late stage; primary and tertiary prevention referenced as sibling topics only
Who does it: clinicians, health systems, and individuals, each named with one line
The honest framing: secondary prevention is the early-warning system, with the reality check that no test is perfect
supporting: The WHO glossary's own examples for secondary prevention: screening and other early detection programs such as routine health checks

claims.claim: The WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021) describes secondary prevention as directed towards early detection of existing disease with a view to arresting or delaying the progression of the disease and its effects, for example through screening and other early detection programs such as routine health checks.

The same glossary frames disease prevention as a whole as measures that reduce the occurrence of risk factors, prevent the occurrence of disease, arrest its progress, and reduce its consequences once established, which places secondary prevention between primary and tertiary along the course of disease.

Primary prevention is directed towards lowering the prevalence of risk factors common to a range of diseases (such as tobacco and alcohol use, obesity and high blood pressure) in order to prevent the initial occurrence of a disorder.
Tertiary prevention generally refers to disease management strategies and/or rehabilitation intended to avoid or reduce the risk of deterioration or complications from established disease.
Screenings are tests that look for diseases before you have symptoms, and screening tests can find diseases early, when they are easier to treat.
Which screening tests a person needs depends on their age, sex, family history, and whether they have risk factors for certain diseases.

Cancer screening means checking for cancer (or for abnormal cells that may become cancer) in people who have no symptoms, and several screening tests have been shown to detect cancer early and to reduce the chance of dying from that cancer.

Screening has trade-offs: false-positive results are possible, false-negative results are possible, and overdiagnosis can find cancers that would never have caused symptoms or harm; finding the cancer may not improve the person's health or help the person live longer.
When abnormal tissue or cancer is found early, it may be easier to treat or cure; by the time symptoms appear, the cancer may have grown and spread, which can make it harder to treat or cure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Screening clearly saves lives versus screening clearly causes harm.
positions: NCI states that several screening tests have been shown to detect cancer early and to reduce the chance of dying from that cancer.
The same NCI source lists false-positive results, false-negative results, and overdiagnosis as possible outcomes of screening.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as true at once: screening helps populations on average by shifting diagnosis earlier, while every individual test carries real trade-offs. This balance is the lesson's honest framing section, not a hedge.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether secondary prevention covers early treatment or only early detection.
positions: Some descriptions define secondary prevention narrowly as early detection and screening.
The WHO glossary frames secondary prevention as early detection with a view to arresting or delaying progression, so detection and treatment are one continuous aim.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the WHO glossary's framing and presents screening tests, early diagnosis, and early treatment as the three tools of one chain, with the glossary as the attributed source.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims; its boilerplate (for example, describing secondary prevention as a foundational concept students use to organize information) carried no evidence and was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic-draft boilerplate with source-verified content; the draft contained no definition, no tools, no examples, and no sources for secondary prevention.
